--- See a feature in an app that you want in your own product? Ask your agent to investigate it with REA. It can inspect the app without its source code, explain how the feature works, show the evidence, and build a version for your project. REA connects your agent to tools for inspecting native binaries, JavaScript and Electron apps, .NET assemblies, and websites. You can also use the same tools from your terminal. Analysis runs locally, and results include the evidence and limitations behind each conclusion. Setup registers REA with your agent and installs matching workflow instructions. Native analysis can use an existing Hopper, Ghidra, IDA or Kuna installation; setup can optionally install Hopper with approval. Static JavaScript analysis needs no native analysis engine. > **[Visit the REA website](https://rea.tools/)** for setup instructions, illustrated guides, and real case studies. ## Quick start On Linux, Ghidra, JADX, firmware tool launches and static JavaScript/Electron analysis require a procps-compatible `ps` on REA's `PATH` for process ownership checks. Recovery steps are in `docs/getting-started/installation.md` under "Linux owned-process prerequisite". ### Set up your agent With Node.js and npm installed, run: ```bash npx rea-agents setup ``` Choose your agents, review the proposed changes, and approve them. Setup adds REA's MCP server and matching workflow instructions, with backups of existing configuration. Restart your agent afterward. Setup records the selected runtime and REA entry script directly. If acquired through a package runner, keep its cache entry available. Run package acquisition from a trusted directory outside the target project. Installation and recovery details are in the setup guide below. Setup supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build and [other agents](docs/getting-started/installation.md#supported-agents). See [installation and setup](docs/getting-started/installation.md) for provider configuration, manual MCP registration, Claude Code/Codex plugins, and the Cursor Marketplace plugin. MCP uses compact input schemas by default to reduce context overhead. Set `REA_MCP_INPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE=full` in your MCP registration when you need the complete advertised field guidance and nested validation details. Both profiles keep the full tool set and canonical server validation. See "Compact input schema profile" in the MCP contracts guide. Complete output schemas are advertised by default. If your client caps the complete `tools/list` frame, set `REA_MCP_OUTPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE=compact` to bound each advertised output schema, or `off` to omit output schemas entirely. Both settings keep canonical server-side validation and complete structured results. See "Output schemas" in the MCP contracts guide. ### Ask your agent ```text Understand how search works in the Notes app, show me the evidence, and build a similar feature for my project. ``` Replace Notes with your target app and the feature you want to understand. ### Use the terminal Inspect an extracted JavaScript/Electron app directory or ASAR: ```bash npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json ``` The result includes modules, imports, Electron boundaries and their evidence. Replace the path with your target, such as `"D:/apps/example"` on Windows. To install the `rea` command for regular use: ```bash npm install --global rea-agents rea --help ``` For native analysis, configure a provider first. See the [CLI and Evidence guide](docs/getting-started/cli.md) for native commands, provider selection, snapshots and scripting. ### Update REA REA changes quickly, and new releases include frequent bug fixes. Keep your installation up to date. For a CLI installed with `npm install --global` or `bun add --global`: ```bash rea update ``` `rea --update` is an alias for this verified workflow and accepts the same global output flags. Use `rea update` when combining it with other command controls. Updater commands retain at most 4 MiB of stdout and stderr combined. Oversized metadata replies are rejected after the command exits; verbose installs continue with bounded diagnostics. Human progress output respects terminal backpressure and waits for submitted writes to finish. Bun global updates require Bun 1.2.17 or later. With an older Bun release, upgrade Bun manually before running `rea update`. To refresh your agent registrations and skill, run the setup command printed by the update. If you use `npx`, update your agent setup with: ```bash npx rea-agents@latest setup ``` Review the setup changes and restart your agent. For one-off CLI commands, use `npx rea-agents@latest` followed by the command. With Bun, use `bunx rea-agents@latest` in place of `npx rea-agents@latest`. ## How REA works Your agent calls REA through MCP to inspect the target and trace relevant code. REA returns findings with their evidence. The agent uses them to ask follow-up questions, explain the behavior, or write and test an implementation. CLI commands use the same workflows. ![REA investigation flow: your agent asks about a local target, REA inspects and traces it using analysis tools, and the agent uses the returned code, references and unknowns to explain, implement and test.](website/public/assets/figures/rea-investigation-flow.svg) [Open the full-size figure](website/public/assets/figures/rea-investigation-flow.svg). ## What you can analyze REA requires Node.js 22.x (>=22.23.4), 24.x (>=24.22.1), or 26.12.1+, plus npm.
